1. Overview¶

Every payment transfer or claim has to pass this Y/N question: Is this Fraud?

2.2 Data Cleaning¶

2.2.1 Missing Values Analysis¶

Missing values can affect the performance of machine learning models:

  • Algorithmic crashes: if the models in learning libraries (i.e Scikit-Learn's Logistic Regression) do not handle missing values, the training process will crash.
  • Hidden Bias: if the missing values are not handled properly, the model may learn patterns that are not representative of the real-world data, leading to biased predictions.
In [5]:
missing_val_counts = df.isnull().sum()
print(missing_val_counts[missing_val_counts>0].index.to_list())

[]

The dataset contains no missing values.

  • No imputation is required
  • The dataset is ready for further preprocessing and analysis.

2.2.2 Duplicate records analysis¶

Duplicate transactions could skew the model performance by causing certain patterns to be overrepresented in the training process. So if there are any duplicated rows presented, they will be removed

  • Reduce bias: as if a specific fraudulent transaction is duplicated 10 times, the model will see that exact pattern repeatedly
  • Improve model generalisation (the ability of your model to perform well on new, unseen data): as the model might just memorise the rows
  • Prevent information leakage: if we split your data into a training set and a testing set without removing duplicates first, the same row might exist in both sets.
In [6]:
duplicated_rows = df.duplicated().sum()
print(f'Number of duplicated rows: {duplicated_rows}')

df = df.drop_duplicates()
df.shape

2.2.3 Class Distribution Analysis¶

Fraud detection is an imbalanced classification problem as most transactions are legitimate, while only a very small fraction are fraudulent.

Therefore, we need to examine the class distribution to understand:

  • Severity of imbalance
  • Need for resampling techniques
  • Expected modeling challenges
In [7]:
print(df['Class'].value_counts(normalize=False))

Class
0    283253
1       473
Name: count, dtype: int64
In [8]:
print(df['Class'].value_counts(normalize=True))

Class
0    0.998333
1    0.001667
Name: proportion, dtype: float64

As it is said, the dataset is highly unbalanced/low prevalence, the positive class (frauds) account only for 0.167% of all transactions (after removing duplicates).

The greater the imbalance, the more challenging it becomes for machine learning models to correctly identify fraudulent cases.

Given the class imbalance ratio, confusion matrix accuracy is not meaningful for unbalanced classification because if a model predicts non-fraud for all transaction, it will achieve an accuracy of 99.8% as fraudulent transactions represents less than 0.2% of the total in our dataset.

$$\text{Accuracy} = \frac{\text{True Positives} + \text{True Negatives}}{\text{Total Predictions}}$$

So we need metrics that focus on the minority class such as:

  • Precision: $$\text{Precision} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP + FP}}$$ → Of all transactions predicted as fraud, how many were actually fraudulent?
  • Recall: $$\text{Recall} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP + FN}}$$ → Of all actual fraud cases, how many did we correctly identify?
  • F1 Score: $$\text{F1 Score} = 2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$$ → The combined metric of both Precision and Recall that penalises extreme values
  • ROC-AUC (Receiver Operating Characteristic - Area Under Curve): plots the True Positive Rate (Recall) against the False Positive Rate ($FPR = \frac{FP}{FP + TN}$) at various threshold settings
  • PR-AUC (Precision-Recall Area Under Curve): plots Precision vs Recall at various threshold settings.

2.3 Data Exploration¶

  • Multicollinearity can make it hard for the model to determine which feature is actually responsible for the prediction. Therefore, we perform a correlation analysis below:
In [9]:
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.heatmap(df.corr(), cmap='crest', annot=False)
plt.title("Correlation Heatmap")
plt.show()

The correlation heatmap shows that deep dark blue represents strong linear correlation between variables, while teal/green colors represents weak linear correlation.

Here, we dont see much deep blue blocks outside the diagonal, so there are no signs of multicollinearity.

=> We can keep all features.

However, most of the V features also appear to have very weak correlations with Class (response variable), which means the fraud signals are likely to be non-linear and cannot be captured by this simple correlation heatmap.

=> We should also test different models that are able to capture non-linear relationships like Random Forests, XGBoost, etc.

We also plot the correlation between the features and the response variable Class to see which features are more correlated with the target variable.

    sns.boxplot(x='Class', y = feature, data = df, ax= axes[i], showfliers=False)
    axes[i].set_title(f'{feature} Distribution')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
  • Strong separators: V14, V12, V10, V17, V4, V11, V3, V16 show visibly different medians and spreads between the two classes (e.g. V14 sits near 0 for legitimate transactions but drops to roughly -7 for fraud). These are the features most likely to carry real predictive weight, and a natural set to watch closely in later feature-importance results.
  • Weak separators: V13, V15, V22, V23, V24, V25, V26 show near-identical boxes for both classes. There features show little to no discriminating power on their own.
  • Time overlaps heavily between classes, which means transaction timing alone doesn't strongly indicate fraud in this dataset.
  • Amount is actually lower on average for fraud than for legitimate transactions. This is worth noting since it runs counter to the common assumption that fraud means unusually large purchases.

This is a useful sanity check to carry into modeling, especially when a trained model's feature importances don't roughly agree with this list (e.g. if V13/V15/V22-V26 show up as highly important), then that's worth a second look, because it could mean the model is picking up an interaction/non-linear effect these single-feature boxplots can't show, or it could be a sign of an issue like leakage or overfitting.

In [13]:
df['log_amount'] = np.log1p(df['Amount']) # log1p means log(amount + 1) as log(0) = undefined so log(1+0) = 0 for transactions with amount equals 0

plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
sns.histplot(data=df, x='log_amount', hue='Class', bins=50, stat='density', common_norm=False, alpha=0.5)
plt.title('Log(Amount) Distribution by Class')
plt.xlabel('Log(Amount)')
plt.show()

Fraud (orange) is sharply concentrated in two narrow spike:

  • Around log_amount ≈ 0.7 (which is Amount ≈ e^0.7 - 1 ≈ $1)

  • Around log_amount ≈ 4.5-5 (roughly Amount ≈ $90-150). Outside these two spikes, fraud density drops close to zero.

Legitimate transactions (blue) are much more spread out and distributed fairly evenly across the whole range from log_amount ≈ 0 up through ≈ 6-7 (roughly $1 to over $1000).

=> Fraudulent transactions in this dataset aren't randomly sized like legitimate ones, they cluster heavily around a couple of specific amount levels, especially very small amounts (~$1). This is might be a fraud pattern that fraudsters first test a stolen card with a tiny charge (like $1) before attempting larger charges, to check if the card is still active/valid without triggering suspicion. The secondary spike around $90-150 could reflect a common "safe" charge amount fraudsters use once a card is validated.

From previous EDA, we conclude to keep all features, so for our machine learning model, we will assign the variables as below:

  • Features (Time, Amount, V1 .. V28, log_amount) → X

=> Here, as all features are numerical values, we dont have to separate numericals and categorical features.

4. Train-Test Split¶

We will divide the dataset into:

  • Training set: for the model to learn patterns of transactions from historical data

  • Testing set: to evaluate the model performance on unseen data if the model is able to capture the patterns successfully

  • In this case, we wont split further into validation set even the data is large enough (>200,000 records) because the proportion of fraud cases in our data is super tiny. Further splitting might make the model harder to capture the patterns of fraudulent.

  • We will perform a stratified split as it is able to preserve the original class distribution in both datasets, i.e it forces the percentage of fraud to be the same in both training set and test set.

P/s: If we are going to use a validation set, it is better to split into training and validation sets before data exploration. If we are using cross validation this is not necessary.

In [15]:
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.20, # 20% of the data is for testing, 80% for training
    random_state=42,
    stratify=y # strify on y
)

print("Training Set :", X_train.shape)
print("Testing Set :", X_test.shape)

5. Feature Scaling¶

Only Time and Amount feature need scaling here, as V1-V28 features are already PCA-transformed. There are four common feature scaling options:

1. StandardScaler (Z-Score Normalization)¶

Rescales to mean 0, standard deviation 1. Assumes roughly normal data.

$$x_{scaled} = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$

Example: average height 170cm, std 10cm -> a height of 180cm becomes 1.0, 160cm becomes -1.0.

Use when: the default choice for most algorithms, especially the distance-based ones (KNN, SVM, PCA) or those assuming normally distributed data (Linear/Logistic Regression).

2. MinMaxScaler (Normalization)¶

Compresses everything into a fixed range, usually [0, 1]. Preserves the original distribution's shape but strictly bounds the extremes.

$$x_{scaled} = \frac{x - x_{min}}{x_{max} - x_{min}}$$

Example: pixel brightness 0-255 -> a value of 127.5 becomes exactly 0.5.

Use when: the data has known, strict bounds, isn't normally distributed, or the algorithm needs positive-only inputs (e.g. image processing, Naive Bayes). Highly sensitive to outliers.

3. RobustScaler¶

Ignores the mean and extremes. Centers on the median, scales by the IQR (middle 50% of the data).

$$x_{scaled} = \frac{x - \text{median}}{\text{IQR}}$$

Example: an income dataset with a billionaire -> the mean gets dragged upward by that one value, but RobustScaler ignores it entirely, scaling based only on the middle class's spread. The billionaire's scaled value just becomes a large number, without distorting everyone else's scale.

Use when: the data has significant outliers you can't (or shouldn't) delete, but you don't want them compressing the scale for everything else.

4. MaxAbsScaler¶

Scales by the absolute maximum value, shifting everything into [-1, 1] without moving the center (a zero stays exactly zero).

$$x_{scaled} = \frac{x}{\max(|x|)}$$

Example: values ranging -50 to 100 -> max absolute value is 100 -> -50 becomes -0.5, 100 becomes 1.0.

Use when: working with sparse data (mostly zeros, e.g. TF-IDF text features). As it doesn't shift the mean, it won't turn millions of meaningful zeros into non-zero decimals.

In this case, Amount is heavily right-skewed with real outliers, which is confirmed in Section 2.3's EDA, where the log-transformed distribution showed fraud clustering sharply around specific values (~$1, ~$90-150) against a much broader, multi-modal spread for legitimate transactions, and the raw boxplots showed Amount dominated by a long tail of large values. Time is less dramatically skewed but it is not close to normally distributed neither, which rules out StandardScaler as the natural choice.

Between the two outlier-tolerant options, RobustScaler fits better than MinMaxScaler here because MinMaxScaler is highly sensitive to outliers (a single extreme Amount value would stretch the entire scale), compressing the vast majority of (normal-range) transactions into a tiny sliver near 0. RobustScaler's median/IQR centering means the handful of very large transactions don't distort how every other transaction gets scaled, exactly the property needed when outliers are expected and meaningful (as they are in fraud data), not something to be engineered away.

In [17]:
numeric_features = ['Time','Amount']
preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers = [
        (
        'num',
        RobustScaler(),
        numeric_features
        )
    ],
    remainder= 'passthrough'
    )

6. Model Selection¶

  • We will test different models to find the best one for our dataset. The models we will test include:
    • Logistic Regression
    • Random Forest Classifier
    • XGBoost Classifier

6.1 Logistic Regression¶

  • Logistic Regression is one of the most widely used algorithms for binary classification. Because fraud detection is a binary classification problem, Logistic Regression serves as an excellent starting point for performance comparison.

Advantages:

  • Fast training
  • Interpretable coefficients
  • Strong baseline model
  • Produces probability estimates

SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique): is a popular technique for handling imbalanced datasets, especially in classification problems like fraud detection. It works by generating synthetic samples of the minority class (in this case, fraudulent transactions) to balance the class distribution.

  • Reduce class imbalance, which can help improve model performance and reduce bias towards the majority class.
  • Improve minority class learning
  • Improve Precision, Recall, and F1 Score by providing the model with more examples of the minority class to learn from.
In [18]:
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline as ImbPipeline
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE

lr_pipeline = ImbPipeline([
    (
        'preprocessor',
        preprocessor
    ),
    (
        'smote',
        SMOTE(random_state=42)
        
    ),
    (
        'model',
        LogisticRegression(
            random_state= 42,
            max_iter= 1000
        )
    )
])

            solver
            
            solver: {'lbfgs', 'liblinear', 'newton-cg', 'newton-cholesky', 'sag', 'saga'},             default='lbfgs'

Algorithm to use in the optimization problem. Default is 'lbfgs'.
To choose a solver, you might want to consider the following aspects:

- 'lbfgs' is a good default solver because it works reasonably well for a wide
  class of problems.
- For :term:`multiclass` problems (`n_classes >= 3`), all solvers except
  'liblinear' minimize the full multinomial loss, 'liblinear' will raise an
  error.
- 'newton-cholesky' is a good choice for
  `n_samples` >> `n_features * n_classes`, especially with one-hot encoded
  categorical features with rare categories. Be aware that the memory usage
  of this solver has a quadratic dependency on `n_features * n_classes`
  because it explicitly computes the full Hessian matrix.
- For small datasets, 'liblinear' is a good choice, whereas 'sag'
  and 'saga' are faster for large ones;
- 'liblinear' can only handle binary classification by default. To apply a
  one-versus-rest scheme for the multiclass setting one can wrap it with the
  :class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier`.

.. warning::
   The choice of the algorithm depends on the penalty chosen (`l1_ratio=0`
   for L2-penalty, `l1_ratio=1` for L1-penalty and `0 < l1_ratio < 1` for
   Elastic-Net) and on (multinomial) multiclass support:

   ================= ======================== ======================
   solver            l1_ratio                 multinomial multiclass
   ================= ======================== ======================
   'lbfgs'           l1_ratio=0               yes
   'liblinear'       l1_ratio=1 or l1_ratio=0 no
   'newton-cg'       l1_ratio=0               yes
   'newton-cholesky' l1_ratio=0               yes
   'sag'             l1_ratio=0               yes
   'saga'            0<=l1_ratio<=1           yes
   ================= ======================== ======================

.. note::
   'sag' and 'saga' fast convergence is only guaranteed on features
   with approximately the same scale. You can preprocess the data with
   a scaler from :mod:`sklearn.preprocessing`.

.. seealso::
   Refer to the :ref:`User Guide <Logistic_regression>` for more
   information regarding :class:`LogisticRegression` and more specifically the
   :ref:`Table <logistic_regression_solvers>`
   summarizing solver/penalty supports.

.. versionadded:: 0.17
   Stochastic Average Gradient (SAG) descent solver. Multinomial support in
   version 0.18.
.. versionadded:: 0.19
   SAGA solver.
.. versionchanged:: 0.22
   The default solver changed from 'liblinear' to 'lbfgs' in 0.22.
.. versionadded:: 1.2
   newton-cholesky solver. Multinomial support in version 1.6.


'lbfgs'

6.1.1 Training Logistic Regression Model¶
The model is trained on the original (imbalanced) training split. SMOTE is applied inside the pipeline during .fit(), so oversampling only ever happens on the training data, never on the test set.


The objective is to learn patterns that distinguish fraudulent transactions from legitimate transactions, and to prevent data leakage in cross-validation in the later stages.


















In [20]:






lr_pipeline.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train
)

                 ColumnTransformer(remainder='passthrough',
                                   transformers=[('num', RobustScaler(),
                                                  ['Time', 'Amount'])])),
                ('smote', SMOTE(random_state=42)),
                ('model', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=42))])

Parameters








            transformers
            
            transformers: list of tuples

List of (name, transformer, columns) tuples specifying the
transformer objects to be applied to subsets of the data.

name : str
    Like in Pipeline and FeatureUnion, this allows the transformer and
    its parameters to be set using ``set_params`` and searched in grid
    search.
transformer : {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator
    Estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
    Special-cased strings 'drop' and 'passthrough' are accepted as
    well, to indicate to drop the columns or to pass them through
    untransformed, respectively.
columns :  str, array-like of str, int, array-like of int,                 array-like of bool, slice or callable
    Indexes the data on its second axis. Integers are interpreted as
    positional columns, while strings can reference DataFrame columns
    by name.  A scalar string or int should be used where
    ``transformer`` expects X to be a 1d array-like (vector),
    otherwise a 2d array will be passed to the transformer.
    A callable is passed the input data `X` and can return any of the
    above. To select multiple columns by name or dtype, you can use
    :obj:`make_column_selector`.


[('num', ...)]







            remainder
            
            remainder: {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator, default='drop'

By default, only the specified columns in `transformers` are
transformed and combined in the output, and the non-specified
columns are dropped. (default of ``'drop'``).
By specifying ``remainder='passthrough'``, all remaining columns that
were not specified in `transformers`, but present in the data passed
to `fit` will be automatically passed through. This subset of columns
is concatenated with the output of the transformers. For dataframes,
extra columns not seen during `fit` will be excluded from the output
of `transform`.
By setting ``remainder`` to be an estimator, the remaining
non-specified columns will use the ``remainder`` estimator. The
estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Note that using this feature requires that the DataFrame columns
input at :term:`fit` and :term:`transform` have identical order.


'passthrough'







            sparse_threshold
            
            sparse_threshold: float, default=0.3

If the output of the different transformers contains sparse matrices,
these will be stacked as a sparse matrix if the overall density is
lower than this value. Use ``sparse_threshold=0`` to always return
dense.  When the transformed output consists of all dense data, the
stacked result will be dense, and this keyword will be ignored.


0.3







            n_jobs
            
            n_jobs: int, default=None

Number of jobs to run in parallel.
``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
for more details.


None







            transformer_weights
            
            transformer_weights: dict, default=None

Multiplicative weights for features per transformer. The output of the
transformer is multiplied by these weights. Keys are transformer names,
values the weights.


None







            verbose
            
            verbose: bool, default=False

If True, the time elapsed while fitting each transformer will be
printed as it is completed.


False







            verbose_feature_names_out
            
            verbose_feature_names_out: bool, str or Callable[[str, str], str], default=True

- If True, :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will prefix
  all feature names with the name of the transformer that generated that
  feature. It is equivalent to setting
  `verbose_feature_names_out="{transformer_name}__{feature_name}"`.
- If False, :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will not
  prefix any feature names and will error if feature names are not
  unique.
- If ``Callable[[str, str], str]``,
  :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will rename all the features
  using the name of the transformer. The first argument of the callable is the
  transformer name and the second argument is the feature name. The returned
  string will be the new feature name.
- If ``str``, it must be a string ready for formatting. The given string will
  be formatted using two field names: ``transformer_name`` and ``feature_name``.
  e.g. ``"{feature_name}__{transformer_name}"``. See :meth:`str.format` method
  from the standard library for more info.

            copy

If `False`, try to avoid a copy and do inplace scaling instead.

not a NumPy array or scipy.sparse CSR matrix, a copy may still be
returned.


True







            unit_variance
            
            unit_variance: bool, default=False

If `True`, scale data so that normally distributed features have a
variance of 1. In general, if the difference between the x-values of
`q_max` and `q_min` for a standard normal distribution is greater
than 1, the dataset will be scaled down. If less than 1, the dataset
will be scaled up.

   ================= ======================== ======================
   solver            l1_ratio                 multinomial multiclass
   ================= ======================== ======================
   'lbfgs'           l1_ratio=0               yes
   'liblinear'       l1_ratio=1 or l1_ratio=0 no
   'newton-cg'       l1_ratio=0               yes
   'newton-cholesky' l1_ratio=0               yes
   'sag'             l1_ratio=0               yes
   'saga'            0<=l1_ratio<=1           yes
   ================= ======================== ======================

.. note::
   'sag' and 'saga' fast convergence is only guaranteed on features
   with approximately the same scale. You can preprocess the data with
   a scaler from :mod:`sklearn.preprocessing`.

6.1.2 Model Evaluation Metrics¶
The following metrics are used:


    

  • Precision
    • 

  • Recall
    • 

  • F1 Score
    • 

  • ROC-AUC
    • 

  • PR-AUC
    • 



These metrics provide a more reliable evaluation than accuracy for highly imbalanced datasets.

Confusion Matrix¶
The confusion matrix reveals how effectively the model distinguishes fraudulent transactions from legitimate ones.


    

  • True Positives: means high successful number of frauds detected.
    • 

  • False Negatives: represent missed fraud cases (Actual frauds but predicted as non-fraud).
    • 

  • False Positives: represent false fraud alert (Legitimate transactions but predicted as fraud).
    • 



Depends on the system, there will be different priorities, either to minimize False Negatives or False Positives or maximize overall accuracy. So depending on the priority, we will need to adjust the threshold for classification accordingly. But in this fraud detection system, a large number of False Negatives will decrease customer satisfaction and trust in the system, while a large number of False Positives will increase business cost to double check whether the transaction is real fraud. Therefore, we want to balance both False Negatives and False Positives, by focusing on optimizing the F1 Score to ensure a balanced approach to fraud detection.


















In [23]:






lr_cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, lr_pred)
lr_cm_disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix= lr_cm, display_labels= ['Non-Fraud (0)', 'Fraud (1)'])
lr_cm_disp.plot(cmap = 'Blues')
plt.title('Confusion Matrix | Logistic Regression')
plt.show()

ROC-AUC measures the model's ability to separate fraud and non-fraud transactions.

6.1.3 Cross-Validated Threshold Selection¶
Classification models output probabilities rather than direct class predictions.


By default, a threshold of 0.50 is used:


    

  • Probability > 0.50 → Fraud
    • 

  • Probability ≤ 0.50 → Non-Fraud
    • 



However, for imbalanced datasets this threshold is often suboptimal.


=> Threshold optimization helps identify the threshold that maximizes model performance, particularly the F1 Score.


To avoid data leakage, threshold optimization should be performed on the validation set or using cross-validation, not on the test set.


=> We use stratified k-fold cross-validation to find the optimal threshold for our model. This approach ensures that each fold maintains the original class distribution, providing a more reliable estimate of model performance across different thresholds.


















In [28]:






from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_predict

skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits = 5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

y_train_prob = cross_val_predict(
    estimator= lr_pipeline, 
    X = X_train,
    y = y_train,
    cv = skf,
    method = 'predict_proba'
    )[:,1]

precision, recall, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_train, y_train_prob)

# Calculate f1-score for each threshold (add a tiny number of 1e-10 to prevent dividing by 0)
f1_scores = 2*(precision*recall)/(precision + recall + 1e-10) 

precision, recall, thresholds, f1_scores

6.1.4 Test Evaluation for Tuned Threshold¶
After determining the optimal threshold through cross-validation, we evaluate the model on the test set using this tuned threshold. This final evaluation provides an unbiased assessment of the model's performance on unseen data, ensuring that the results reflect its true predictive capabilities in real-world scenarios.


















In [30]:

print(classification_report(y_test, lr_pred_tuned))

ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm_tuned, display_labels=['Non-Fraud (0)', 'Fraud (1)']).plot(cmap='Blues')

plt.show()

weighted avg       1.00      1.00      1.00     56746





































Findings:







Default threshold (0.5)
Tuned threshold (~0.99999999)






Precision (fraud)
0.05
0.88




Recall (fraud)
0.87
0.73




F1 (fraud)
0.10
0.80






Threshold tuning produced a dramatic, practically meaningful improvement. Translating the ratios into
actual transaction counts (95 fraud cases in the test set):


    

  • At the default 0.5 threshold: recall 0.87 -> ~83 frauds caught, but precision 0.05 means only 5%
of flagged transactions were real fraud -> roughly 83 / 0.05 ~ 1,660 total flagged transactions,
meaning ~1,577 legitimate transactions were wrongly flagged as fraud.
    • 

  • At the tuned threshold: recall 0.73 -> ~69 frauds caught (14 fewer). Precision 0.88 ->
69 / 0.88 ~ 78 total flagged, meaning only ~9 false alarms.
    • 



In plain terms: tuning the threshold cut false alarms by ~99% (from ~1,577 down to ~9), at the cost of catching only 14 fewer actual fraud cases. For a real fraud system, a model flagging 1,660
transactions to investigate (95% of which are false alarms) is operationally useless; flagging 78 transactions with 88% actually being fraud is something an investigations team could realistically act
on.


Why the default threshold performed so poorly — most likely a consequence of SMOTE: training on a
perfectly 50/50 SMOTE-balanced dataset shifts the model's whole notion of "confident." A raw 0.5 cutoff,
calibrated for a balanced training distribution, is far too permissive once applied to real-world data
that's actually ~99.8% legitimate. This is exactly why threshold tuning isn't just helpful but
necessary after using SMOTE for an imbalanced problem like this one.


Note on AUC metrics: ROC-AUC (0.957) and PR-AUC (0.682), computed earlier, are threshold-independent
and therefore unaffected by this tuning step — they summarize the model's ranking quality across every
possible threshold. Only the classification report / confusion matrix numbers shift with the chosen
threshold, since those depend on where exactly the cutoff is drawn.






















We assume it takes roughly 1 hour to review a transaction manually to double check if it is a real fraud and assume the average salary for per hour is $12, then we set review_cost = 12


However,  this assumption matters a lot the "optimal" thresholds and the entire
cost-vs-benefit conclusion below are sensitive to this number. A materially different review cost
(e.g. $5 vs $12) can shift which thresholds come out best, and by how much the bucket-based approach
outperforms a single global threshold. Any real deployment should replace this with an actual
estimated cost from the business (analyst time, tooling, etc.) before trusting the conclusion.






















For Missed Fraud (fn_mask)


When a fraudster succeeds, the bank loses the actual stolen money. Missing a $5,000 fraud hurts the business vastly more than missing a $5 fraud. Therefore, treating every mistake as equal is financially dangerous.


For False Alarms (fp_mask)


When the model flags a legitimate customer, the bank does not lose the transaction amount. It only loses the administrative cost of paying an employee to review the alert (e.g., $12). Reviewing a $5,000 false alarm takes the exact same amount of time as reviewing a $5 false alarm. Here, we do not care about the transaction size, but only care about how many false alarms occurred.


















In [31]:






def total_cost( y_test, y_pred, amounts, review_cost = 12):
    fn_mask = (y_pred == 0) & (y_test == 1) # missed fraud 
    fp_mask = (y_pred == 1) & (y_test == 0) # false alarm

    missed_fraud_cost = amounts[fn_mask].sum() 
    false_alarm_cost = fp_mask.sum() * review_cost

    return missed_fraud_cost + false_alarm_cost





















In [32]:






from itertools import product

amounts = X_train['Amount'].values # .values to return np array, else return pd series

best_cost = float('inf')
best_thres_combi = None

for thres_low, thres_mid, thres_high in product(
    np.arange(0.9, 1.0, 0.01), 
    np.arange(0.8, 1.0, 0.01),
    np.arange(0.6, 1.0, 0.01)
):
    conditions = [
        amounts < 50,
        (amounts >= 50) & (amounts <1000),
        amounts >= 1000
    ]

    applied_threshold = np.select(condlist = conditions, choicelist= [thres_low, thres_mid, thres_high], default  = 0.99)
    y_preds = (y_train_prob >= applied_threshold).astype(int)
    cost = total_cost(y_train.values, y_preds, amounts, review_cost= 12)

    if cost < best_cost:
        best_cost = cost
        best_thres_combi = (thres_low, thres_mid, thres_high)


print("Best thresholds (low, mid, high):", best_thres_combi)
print("Lowest total cost found:", best_cost)

In [33]:






best_low, best_mid, best_high = best_thres_combi

def dynamic_threshold(lr_prob, amount):
    conditions = [amount < 50, (amount >= 50)&(amount < 1000), amount >= 1000]
    applied_threshold = np.select(conditions, best_thres_combi, default = 0.99)
    return (lr_prob >= applied_threshold).astype(int)

y_pred_final = dynamic_threshold(lr_prob, X_test['Amount'].values)   # update dynamic_threshold to use best_combo values

plt.show()

final_test_cost = total_cost(y_test.values, y_pred_final, X_test['Amount'].values, review_cost=12)

Features with negative coefficients push the model to predict towards Class 0 (non-fraud), while positive coefficients push the model to predict towards Class 1 (fraud), because the hypothesis function of logistic regression is a sigmoid function:


$$h_\theta(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\theta^T x}}$$


The odds formula is:


$$\text{Odds} = \frac{P(Class = 1)}{P(Class = 0)} = \frac{P(Class = 1)}{1 - P(Class = 1)} = \frac{h_\theta(x)}{1 - h_\theta(x)} = \frac{\frac{1}{1 + e^{-\theta^T x}}}{1 - \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\theta^T x}}} = \frac{\frac{1}{1 + e^{-\theta^T x}}}{\frac{e^{-\theta^T x}}{1 + e^{-\theta^T x}}} = \frac{1}{e^{-\theta^T x}} = e^{\theta^T x} = e^{\theta_0 + \theta_1 V1 + \theta_2 V2 + ... + \theta_{28} V28}$$


If we increase V4 feature by 1 unit:


$$\text{New Odds} = e^{\theta_4 (V4 + 1) + \theta_0 + \theta_1 V1 + \theta_2 V2 + ... + \theta_{28} V28} = e^{\theta_4} \cdot \text{Old Odds}$$


With V4 coefficient of 0.901430:


    

  • The odd ratio multiplier is e^0.901430 = 2.46, which means that for every 1 unit increase in V4, the odds of a transaction being fraudulent are multiplied by a factor of 2.46 or increase by 146%, holding all other features constant. This indicates that V4 is a strong predictor of fraud in this model.
    • 

  • P(Class = 1) = 1/(1 + e^-0.901430) = 0.288756, which means the model predicts a 28.88% chance that a transaction is Class 1 (fraud) or 71.12% chance that a transaction is Class 0 (non-fraud).
    • 



With V14 coefficient of -0.825:


    

  • The odds multiplier is e^-0.825 = 0.6953, which means that for every 1 unit increase in V14, the odds of a transaction being fraudulent are multiplied by 0.695, a 30.47% decrease, holding all other features constant. A negative coefficient pushes the model toward Class 0 (non-fraud), consistent with the EDA finding that V14 is lower for fraudulent transactions.
    • 























Findings: is the amount-aware bucket approach actually worth the added complexity?







Single global threshold
Amount-aware buckets






Precision (fraud)
0.88
0.47




Recall (fraud)
0.73
0.81




False alarms (approx.)
~9
~87




Total cost (test, $12/review)
$3,967.59
$3,658.86






The bucket approach reduces total cost by ~7.8% (about $309 on the test set) and catches 8 more
fraud cases (77 vs. 69), but it produces roughly 10x more false alarms (about 87 vs. 9) that would
need manual review.


The chosen thresholds:


best_low  = 0.99   (< \$50 bucket)
best_mid  = 0.92   (\$50-\$1000 bucket)
best_high = 0.99   (>= \$1000 bucket)



The lower threshold lands on the mid-range bucket ($50-$1000), while both the smallest (< $50) and largest (>= $1000) buckets sit at 0.99. So the optimizer does not give high-value transactions the more sensitive threshold, and that intuition should not be claimed in the writeup.


Conclusion: under the $12 review-cost assumption, the amount-aware thresholds are cheaper on the test set (about $309 less), but they flag roughly ten times as many legitimate transactions. Whether that trade is worth it depends on the real cost of a manual review, so this should be treated as a sensitivity result rather than a settled conclusion until that cost is validated.






















6.1.6 Section Conclusion | Logistic Regression¶
We built a Logistic Regression pipeline with RobustScaler (for Time/Amount) and
SMOTE inside an imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline, so oversampling only ever happens on the current
training fold, and never leaks synthetic points across cross-validation splits.


Key findings:


    

  1. The default 0.5 threshold performed very poorly (precision 0.05, recall 0.87, F1 0.10).
Training on a 50/50 SMOTE-balanced dataset shifts what "confident" means, the model is trained in a world where fraud is 50% of transactions. So a raw 0.5 cutoff in this case is calibrated for a balanced class split, but when applied to real-world data that's actually ~99.8% legitimate, it becomes far too permissive. So here, the model flags far too many legitimate transactions as fraud, leading to a high number number of false alarms (~1,577).
    

    2. 

  2. Cross-validated threshold tuning was the single highest-leverage fix in this section. Choosing
the threshold via cross_val_predict on the training set (never touching test until the final,
one-time check) raised the threshold to ≈0.9999999939 and produced precision 0.88 / recall 0.73 /
F1 0.80. This cuts the false alarms by roughly 99% (from ~1,577 down to ~9) while missing 14 more
fraud cases than the default threshold caught. So depending on the business's tolerance for missed fraud vs. false alarms, this is a very strong improvement.
    

    3. 

  3. The amount-aware dynamic-threshold experiment is cheaper but noisier. It reduced total estimated cost by about 7.8% (about $309) on the test set, catching 8 more frauds, but at the price of roughly ten times as many false alarms. Whether the trade is worth it depends on the real review cost, which is still an assumption.
    

    4. 























6.2 Random Forest Classifier¶
As the correlation analysis in Section 2.3 shows, the fraud signals are likely to be non-linear and cannot be captured by simple correlation heatmap. Therefore, we will test Random Forest Classifier as it is able to capture non-linear relationships between features and the target variable.

were not specified in `transformers`, but present in the data passed

is concatenated with the output of the transformers. For dataframes,
extra columns not seen during `fit` will be excluded from the output
of `transform`.

non-specified columns will use the ``remainder`` estimator. The
estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.

The minimum number of samples required to split an internal node:

Controls both the randomness of the bootstrapping of the samples used

42







            criterion
            
            criterion: {"gini", "entropy", "log_loss"}, default="gini"

The function to measure the quality of a split. Supported criteria are
"gini" for the Gini impurity and "log_loss" and "entropy" both for the
Shannon information gain, see :ref:`tree_mathematical_formulation`.
Note: This parameter is tree-specific.


'gini'







            min_samples_leaf
            
            min_samples_leaf: int or float, default=1

The minimum number of samples required to be at a leaf node.
A split point at any depth will only be considered if it leaves at
least ``min_samples_leaf`` training samples in each of the left and
right branches.  This may have the effect of smoothing the model,
especially in regression.

- If int, then consider `min_samples_leaf` as the minimum number.
- If float, then `min_samples_leaf` is a fraction and
  `ceil(min_samples_leaf * n_samples)` are the minimum
  number of samples for each node.

   Added float values for fractions.


1







            min_weight_fraction_leaf

The minimum weighted fraction of the sum total of weights (of all

0.0







            max_features
            
            max_features: {"sqrt", "log2", None}, int or float, default="sqrt"

The number of features to consider when looking for the best split:

- If int, then consider `max_features` features at each split.
- If float, then `max_features` is a fraction and
  `max(1, int(max_features * n_features_in_))` features are considered at each
  split.
- If "sqrt", then `max_features=sqrt(n_features)`.
- If "log2", then `max_features=log2(n_features)`.
- If None, then `max_features=n_features`.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
    The default of `max_features` changed from `"auto"` to `"sqrt"`.

Note: the search for a split does not stop until at least one
valid partition of the node samples is found, even if it requires to
effectively inspect more than ``max_features`` features.


'sqrt'







            max_leaf_nodes
            
            max_leaf_nodes: int, default=None

Grow trees with ``max_leaf_nodes`` in best-first fashion.
Best nodes are defined as relative reduction in impurity.
If None then unlimited number of leaf nodes.


None







            min_impurity_decrease
            
            min_impurity_decrease: float, default=0.0

A node will be split if this split induces a decrease of the impurity
greater than or equal to this value.

The weighted impurity decrease equation is the following::

    N_t / N * (impurity - N_t_R / N_t * right_impurity
                        - N_t_L / N_t * left_impurity)

where ``N`` is the total number of samples, ``N_t`` is the number of
samples at the current node, ``N_t_L`` is the number of samples in the
left child, and ``N_t_R`` is the number of samples in the right child.

``N``, ``N_t``, ``N_t_R`` and ``N_t_L`` all refer to the weighted sum,
if ``sample_weight`` is passed.

.. versionadded:: 0.19


0.0

custom metric. Only available if `bootstrap=True`.

For an illustration of out-of-bag (OOB) error estimation, see the example
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_ensemble_oob.py`.

False







            class_weight
            
            class_weight: {"balanced", "balanced_subsample"}, dict or list of dicts,             default=None

Weights associated with classes in the form ``{class_label: weight}``.
If not given, all classes are supposed to have weight one. For
multi-output problems, a list of dicts can be provided in the same
order as the columns of y.

Note that for multioutput (including multilabel) weights should be
defined for each class of every column in its own dict. For example,
for four-class multilabel classification weights should be
[{0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 5}, {0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 1}] instead of
[{1:1}, {2:5}, {3:1}, {4:1}].

The "balanced" mode uses the values of y to automatically adjust
weights inversely proportional to class frequencies in the input data
as ``n_samples / (n_classes * np.bincount(y))``

The "balanced_subsample" mode is the same as "balanced" except that
weights are computed based on the bootstrap sample for every tree
grown.

For multi-output, the weights of each column of y will be multiplied.

Note that these weights will be multiplied with sample_weight (passed
through the fit method) if sample_weight is specified.


None







            ccp_alpha
            
            ccp_alpha: non-negative float, default=0.0

Complexity parameter used for Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning. The
subtree with the largest cost complexity that is smaller than
``ccp_alpha`` will be chosen. By default, no pruning is performed. See
:ref:`minimal_cost_complexity_pruning` for details. See
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_tree_plot_cost_complexity_pruning.py`
for an example of such pruning.

.. versionadded:: 0.22


0.0







            max_samples
            
            max_samples: int or float, default=None

If bootstrap is True, the number of samples to draw from X
to train each base estimator.

- If None (default), then draw `X.shape[0]` samples irrespective of
  `sample_weight`.
- If int, then draw `max_samples` samples.
- If float, then draw `max_samples * X.shape[0]` unweighted samples
  or `max_samples * sample_weight.sum()` weighted samples.

.. versionadded:: 0.22

.. versionchanged:: 1.9
    Float `max_samples` is relative to `sample_weight.sum()` instead of
    `X.shape[0]` for weighted samples.


None







            monotonic_cst
            
            monotonic_cst: array-like of int of shape (n_features), default=None

Indicates the monotonicity constraint to enforce on each feature.
  - 1: monotonic increase
  - 0: no constraint
  - -1: monotonic decrease

If monotonic_cst is None, no constraints are applied.

Monotonicity constraints are not supported for:
  - multiclass classifications (i.e. when `n_classes > 2`),
  - multioutput classifications (i.e. when `n_outputs_ > 1`).

The constraints hold over the probability of the positive class.

Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <monotonic_cst_gbdt>`.

.. versionadded:: 1.4

Parameters








            n_estimators
            
            n_estimators: int, default=100

The number of trees in the forest.

.. versionchanged:: 0.22
   The default value of ``n_estimators`` changed from 10 to 100
   in 0.22.


200







            max_depth
            
            max_depth: int, default=None

The maximum depth of the tree. If None, then nodes are expanded until
all leaves are pure or until all leaves contain less than
min_samples_split samples.


8







            min_samples_split
            
            min_samples_split: int or float, default=2

The minimum number of samples required to split an internal node:

- If int, then consider `min_samples_split` as the minimum number.
- If float, then `min_samples_split` is a fraction and
  `ceil(min_samples_split * n_samples)` are the minimum
  number of samples for each split.

.. versionchanged:: 0.18
   Added float values for fractions.


5







            random_state
            
            random_state: int, RandomState instance or None, default=None

Controls both the randomness of the bootstrapping of the samples used
when building trees (if ``bootstrap=True``) and the sampling of the
features to consider when looking for the best split at each node
(if ``max_features < n_features``).
See :term:`Glossary <random_state>` for details.


42







            criterion
            
            criterion: {"gini", "entropy", "log_loss"}, default="gini"

The function to measure the quality of a split. Supported criteria are
"gini" for the Gini impurity and "log_loss" and "entropy" both for the
Shannon information gain, see :ref:`tree_mathematical_formulation`.
Note: This parameter is tree-specific.


'gini'







            min_samples_leaf
            
            min_samples_leaf: int or float, default=1

The minimum number of samples required to be at a leaf node.
A split point at any depth will only be considered if it leaves at
least ``min_samples_leaf`` training samples in each of the left and
right branches.  This may have the effect of smoothing the model,
especially in regression.

- If int, then consider `min_samples_leaf` as the minimum number.
- If float, then `min_samples_leaf` is a fraction and
  `ceil(min_samples_leaf * n_samples)` are the minimum
  number of samples for each node.

.. versionchanged:: 0.18
   Added float values for fractions.


1







            min_weight_fraction_leaf
            
            min_weight_fraction_leaf: float, default=0.0

The minimum weighted fraction of the sum total of weights (of all
the input samples) required to be at a leaf node. Samples have
equal weight when sample_weight is not provided.


0.0







            max_features
            
            max_features: {"sqrt", "log2", None}, int or float, default="sqrt"

The number of features to consider when looking for the best split:

- If int, then consider `max_features` features at each split.
- If float, then `max_features` is a fraction and
  `max(1, int(max_features * n_features_in_))` features are considered at each
  split.
- If "sqrt", then `max_features=sqrt(n_features)`.
- If "log2", then `max_features=log2(n_features)`.
- If None, then `max_features=n_features`.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
    The default of `max_features` changed from `"auto"` to `"sqrt"`.

Note: the search for a split does not stop until at least one
valid partition of the node samples is found, even if it requires to
effectively inspect more than ``max_features`` features.


'sqrt'







            max_leaf_nodes
            
            max_leaf_nodes: int, default=None

Grow trees with ``max_leaf_nodes`` in best-first fashion.
Best nodes are defined as relative reduction in impurity.
If None then unlimited number of leaf nodes.


None







            min_impurity_decrease
            
            min_impurity_decrease: float, default=0.0

A node will be split if this split induces a decrease of the impurity
greater than or equal to this value.

The weighted impurity decrease equation is the following::

    N_t / N * (impurity - N_t_R / N_t * right_impurity
                        - N_t_L / N_t * left_impurity)

where ``N`` is the total number of samples, ``N_t`` is the number of
samples at the current node, ``N_t_L`` is the number of samples in the
left child, and ``N_t_R`` is the number of samples in the right child.

``N``, ``N_t``, ``N_t_R`` and ``N_t_L`` all refer to the weighted sum,
if ``sample_weight`` is passed.

.. versionadded:: 0.19


0.0







            bootstrap
            
            bootstrap: bool, default=True

Whether bootstrap samples are used when building trees. If False, the
whole dataset is used to build each tree.


True







            oob_score
            
            oob_score: bool or callable, default=False

Whether to use out-of-bag samples to estimate the generalization score.
By default, :func:`~sklearn.metrics.accuracy_score` is used.
Provide a callable with signature `metric(y_true, y_pred)` to use a
custom metric. Only available if `bootstrap=True`.

For an illustration of out-of-bag (OOB) error estimation, see the example
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_ensemble_oob.py`.


False







            n_jobs
            
            n_jobs: int, default=None

The number of jobs to run in parallel. :meth:`fit`, :meth:`predict`,
:meth:`decision_path` and :meth:`apply` are all parallelized over the
trees. ``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend`
context. ``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary
<n_jobs>` for more details.


None







            verbose
            
            verbose: int, default=0

Controls the verbosity when fitting and predicting.


0







            warm_start
            
            warm_start: bool, default=False

When set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit
and add more estimators to the ensemble, otherwise, just fit a whole
new forest. See :term:`Glossary <warm_start>` and
:ref:`tree_ensemble_warm_start` for details.


False







            class_weight
            
            class_weight: {"balanced", "balanced_subsample"}, dict or list of dicts,             default=None

Weights associated with classes in the form ``{class_label: weight}``.
If not given, all classes are supposed to have weight one. For
multi-output problems, a list of dicts can be provided in the same
order as the columns of y.

Note that for multioutput (including multilabel) weights should be
defined for each class of every column in its own dict. For example,
for four-class multilabel classification weights should be
[{0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 5}, {0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 1}] instead of
[{1:1}, {2:5}, {3:1}, {4:1}].

The "balanced" mode uses the values of y to automatically adjust
weights inversely proportional to class frequencies in the input data
as ``n_samples / (n_classes * np.bincount(y))``

The "balanced_subsample" mode is the same as "balanced" except that
weights are computed based on the bootstrap sample for every tree
grown.

For multi-output, the weights of each column of y will be multiplied.

Note that these weights will be multiplied with sample_weight (passed
through the fit method) if sample_weight is specified.


None







            ccp_alpha
            
            ccp_alpha: non-negative float, default=0.0

Complexity parameter used for Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning. The
subtree with the largest cost complexity that is smaller than
``ccp_alpha`` will be chosen. By default, no pruning is performed. See
:ref:`minimal_cost_complexity_pruning` for details. See
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_tree_plot_cost_complexity_pruning.py`
for an example of such pruning.

.. versionadded:: 0.22


0.0







            max_samples
            
            max_samples: int or float, default=None

If bootstrap is True, the number of samples to draw from X
to train each base estimator.

- If None (default), then draw `X.shape[0]` samples irrespective of
  `sample_weight`.
- If int, then draw `max_samples` samples.
- If float, then draw `max_samples * X.shape[0]` unweighted samples
  or `max_samples * sample_weight.sum()` weighted samples.

.. versionadded:: 0.22

.. versionchanged:: 1.9
    Float `max_samples` is relative to `sample_weight.sum()` instead of
    `X.shape[0]` for weighted samples.


None







            monotonic_cst
            
            monotonic_cst: array-like of int of shape (n_features), default=None

Indicates the monotonicity constraint to enforce on each feature.
  - 1: monotonic increase
  - 0: no constraint
  - -1: monotonic decrease

If monotonic_cst is None, no constraints are applied.

Monotonicity constraints are not supported for:
  - multiclass classifications (i.e. when `n_classes > 2`),
  - multioutput classifications (i.e. when `n_outputs_ > 1`).

The constraints hold over the probability of the positive class.

Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <monotonic_cst_gbdt>`.

.. versionadded:: 1.4


None

plt.show()
















































A ROC AUC score of 0.98 means that if we randomly select one fraud and one non-fraud transaction, the model will correctly rank the fraud as higher risk than the non-fraud 98% of the time. However, this is an imbalanced dataset with a huge amount of True Negatives that drive the False Positive Rate down to tiny values, which makes the area under the ROC curve is massive (0.98). So ROC AUC score is not a good metric to evaluate the model performance in this case. Instead, we will also use Precision-Recall AUC (PR-AUC) to evaluate the model performance.


















In [41]:






rf_pr_auc = average_precision_score(y_test, rf_prob)
PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_estimator(
    estimator = rf_pipeline,
    X = X_test,
    y = y_test,
    name = "PR-AUC"
)

plt.title('Precision-Recall AUC Curve | Random Forest')
plt.grid()
plt.show()
















































The PR-AUC score of 0.76 means that if we average the precision across all recall levels, 76% of the transactions predicted as fraud are actually fraudulent.


We see that the PR-AUC blue line stays relatively flat and high until Recall hits 0.8. After the 0.8 mark, the precision drops sharply, so we can tune the threshold to safely catch 80% of true positive.






















6.2.3 Cross-Validated Threshold Selection¶


















In [42]:






skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

rf_y_prob_train = cross_val_predict(
    estimator= rf_pipeline,
    X = X_train,
    y = y_train,
    cv = skf,
    method = 'predict_proba'
)[:,1]

rf_precision, rf_recall, rf_thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_train, rf_y_prob_train)

rf_f1_scores = 2*(rf_precision*rf_recall)/(rf_precision + rf_recall + 1e-10)

rf_thresholds_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'threshold': rf_thresholds,
    'precision':rf_precision[:-1],
    'recall': rf_recall[:-1],
    'f1_score': rf_f1_scores[:-1] 
})

rf_optimal_threshold = rf_thresholds_df.loc[rf_thresholds_df['f1_score'].idxmax(),'threshold']
print(f"RF optimal threshold: {rf_optimal_threshold:.8f}")

6.2.5 Hyperparameter Tuning¶
We can perform hyperparameter tuning to find the best combination of hyperparameters for the Random Forest model, by using GridSearchCV to search through a predefined set of hyperparameters and evaluate the model performance using cross-validation. However, due to computational constraints, we will not perform it in this notebook.


from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

param_grid = {
    'model__n_estimators' :[200,300,400],
    'model__max_depth': [None, 8, 15],
    'model__min_samples_split': [2,4,6]
}

rf_grid_search = GridSearchCV(
    estimator = rf_pipeline,
    param_grid = param_grid,
    cv = 5,
    scoring = 'average_precision',
    n_jobs = -1, # Uses all CPU cores,
    verbose = 2 # print live progress updates to the consoles
)

rf_grid_search.fit(X_train, y_train)























6.2.6 Section Conclusion | Random Forest Classifier¶
Same as the Logistic Regression pipeline, we built a Random Forest Classifier pipeline with RobustScaler (for Time/Amount) and SMOTE inside an imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline.


Key findings:


    

  1. Random Forest ranks transactions better than Logistic Regression. It has a higher PR-AUC (0.76 vs. 0.68) and ROC-AUC (0.978 vs. 0.957) on the test set.
    2. 

  2. At the tuned threshold, Random Forest and Logistic Regression perform the same. Both reach precision 0.88, recall 0.73, and F1 0.80. The F1 gap seen at the default threshold (0.58 vs. 0.10) reflects default calibration, not model quality, so it should not be used to rank the models.
    3. 

  3. Feature importance is consistent with the EDA and Logistic Regression. After correcting the column-label mapping, the top features are the EDA separators (V14, V10, V12, V4, V11, V17, V3, V16).
    4. 



Conclusion: Random Forest is a better ranker than Logistic Regression, but it does not beat Logistic Regression on tuned F1, precision, or recall, and it costs more under the current assumption.






















6.3 XGBoost Classifier¶
XGBoost is a gradient boosting algorithm that is known for its high performance and efficiency. It builds an ensemble of decision trees in a sequential manner, where each tree tries to correct the errors of the previous one. This makes it particularly effective for imbalanced datasets like fraud detection.






















Instead of using SMOTE, we will also use the scale_pos_weight parameter in XGBoost to handle class imbalance to see if it can achieve better performance than SMOTE.  This parameter adjusts the weight of the positive class (fraud) during training, allowing the model to focus more on correctly classifying fraudulent transactions.






















6.3.1 Training XGBoost Classifier Model¶


















In [45]:






import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
class_count = y_train.value_counts()
weight_ratio = class_count[0]/class_count[1]
xgb_spw_pipeline = Pipeline([
    (
        'preprocessor',
        preprocessor
    ),
    (
        'model',
        xgb.XGBClassifier(
            scale_pos_weight = weight_ratio,
            eval_metric = 'aucpr',
            n_estimators =200,
            max_depth = 5,
            random_state=42
        )
    )
])
    
xgb_spw_pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
xgb_spw_pred = xgb_spw_pipeline.predict(X_test)
xgb_spw_prob = xgb_spw_pipeline.predict_proba(X_test)[:,1]

xgb_smote_pipeline = ImbPipeline([
    (
        'preprocessor',
        preprocessor
    ),
    (
        'smote',
        SMOTE(random_state =42)
    ),
    (
        'model',
        xgb.XGBClassifier(
            n_estimators = 200,
            max_depth = 5,
            random_state = 42
        )
    )
])

xgb_smote_pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
xgb_smote_pred = xgb_smote_pipeline.predict(X_test)
xgb_smote_prob = xgb_smote_pipeline.predict_proba(X_test)[:,1]

Both SMOTE and scale_pos_weight returns better results than the default 0.5 threshold than Logistic Regression's default result
(precision 0.05, recall 0.87, F1 0.10 in 6.1).


However, 'scale_pos_weight' returns better results than SMOTE because it reweights the loss function during training rather than duplicating/synthesizing minority samples the way SMOTE does. This doesn't push predicted probabilities toward the extremes the way SMOTE does.

0.813






scale_pos_weight clearly wins here — noticeably higher precision and F1 at the default threshold,
and modestly better on both AUC metrics, while recall is essentially tied. This confirms the 6.3
intro's suspicion was worth testing, and answers it directly: for XGBoost on this dataset,
reweighting the loss function is a better imbalance strategy than SMOTE oversampling. A plausible explanation is that scale_pos_weight reweights the loss without changing the training distribution, while SMOTE changes it; we did not verify this calibration effect directly here.


Decision: the rest of this section (threshold tuning, feature importance, final evaluation) proceeds
with the scale_pos_weight pipeline (xgb_spw_pipeline) as the better-performing variant; the SMOTE
version is kept above only as the comparison evidence for this decision, not carried forward further.

Unlike Logistic Regression, where cross-validated threshold tuning was the single biggest lever
(F1 0.10 → 0.80), tuning barely moves XGBoost's result at all for scale_pos_weight method, but it does a little for SMOTE with F1 0.79 → 0.84


A likely explanation is that using scale_pos_weight instead of SMOTE leaves the default threshold already close to optimal, so there is little room for threshold tuning to improve on it.

6.3.4 Section Conclusion | XGBoost Classifier¶
We built an XGBoost pipeline with RobustScaler (for Time/Amount) and scale_pos_weight set to the
class ratio, and compared it with a SMOTE variant.


Key findings:


    

  1. scale_pos_weight is the better imbalance strategy for XGBoost here. At the default threshold it
reaches precision 0.94, recall 0.78, and F1 0.85, against 0.79 / 0.79 / 0.79 for SMOTE. It also has
higher ROC-AUC (0.978 vs. 0.967) and PR-AUC (0.816 vs. 0.813).
    2. 

  2. Threshold tuning helps SMOTE more than scale_pos_weight. The tuned SMOTE threshold (0.977) lifts
F1 from 0.79 to 0.84, mainly by raising precision to 0.96. The tuned scale_pos_weight threshold (0.851)
leaves F1 at 0.85.
    3. 

  3. XGBoost has the strongest ranking quality of the three models. Its PR-AUC of 0.816 is the highest,
and its tuned F1 of 0.85 is the highest. Its tuned threshold (0.851) is also more moderate than
Logistic Regression's (≈0.9999999939).
    4. 

  4. Feature importance matches the EDA. With correctly labelled features, V14 dominates, followed by
V4, V12, V10, V3, V8, V19, V17, V7, and V11. These largely overlap with the strongest
separators in Section 2.3. This should be confirmed in the re-run chart.
    5.

Conclusion: XGBoost with scale_pos_weight is the recommended model. It has the best PR-AUC and F1,
and its cost is within about 3% of the cheapest option. Logistic Regression remains the simpler,
slightly cheaper baseline. The SMOTE variant is clearly weaker at the default threshold and benefits
from tuning, but it still does not beat scale_pos_weight.
